name: Thymosin Beta-4
lead: Thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) is a small, abundant peptide of about 43 to 44 amino acids, encoded by the TMSB4X gene on the X chromosome, whose best-established role is binding monomeric actin and so regulating the cell cytoskeleton [1][2][3]. It was first isolated from calf thymus tissue and its amino acid sequence was published in 1981 by the group of Allan Goldstein [4][13].

In looksmaxxing and recovery communities Tβ4, and a synthetic fragment sold as TB-500, is discussed for two kinds of appearance payoff. The first is a recovery chain: faster tissue repair, fewer training interruptions, more consistent lifting, a better physique. The second is hair: mouse and rat studies from the mid-2000s reported that Tβ4 activated hair follicle stem cells and increased hair growth, and users talk about it as a hair peptide [20][21][2]. A third, more speculative thread on looksmax.org proposes it as part of a facial-bone remodelling routine [22].

Outside cells the peptide has been reported to promote cell migration, blood-vessel formation and tissue repair [1]. Phase 2 trials have tested it in skin ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa, dry eye and corneal wounds, and cardiac trials were registered [5][6][7][8]. It has no approved use, the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it, and it became widely known in Australia through the Essendon and Cronulla sports-doping cases [2][23].

paras: Tβ4 binds globular actin in a 1:1 complex and holds a pool of unpolymerised actin available for the cell, a function worked out in cell-biology studies of profilin and actin dynamics [9][10]. Inside cells it is regarded as the principal actin-sequestering protein in many cell types, and intracellular concentrations have been reported to reach about 0.5 millimolar [2]. A 1991 study found that an actin-sequestering peptide called Fx was the same molecule as Tβ4 [19].

Wikipedia describes additional extracellular 'moonlighting' roles: proposed mechanisms include binding to the beta subunit of ATP synthase as a candidate receptor and a cleaved tetrapeptide, Ac-SDKP, with reported effects on cell migration, blood vessel formation, stem-cell maturation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production [2]. The same article notes that knockout mice developed and bred apparently normally, which raises questions about how essential the protein is for development, and that parts of the section carry an original-research tag [2]. The gene escapes X inactivation and has a Y-chromosome homologue, TMSB4Y [2].

Tβ4 was first thought to be a thymic hormone. Goldstein's group prepared thymosin fraction 5 from calf thymus in 1972, and Tβ4 was later purified from it [13]. In 1981 the complete amino acid sequence of bovine Tβ4 was published, making it the second biologically active peptide from that fraction to be fully sequenced and synthesised, after thymosin alpha 1 [4][2]. Researchers subsequently found that it forms a complex with G-actin, and a 1991 study showed it to be identical to Fx [19][2].
The World Health Organization recommended the international nonproprietary name timbetasin for an acetylated form [2]. Clinical development moved into wound-healing trials from about 2006 [5][6].

Researchers studying wound healing observed faster hair growth near wound edges and then reported in 2004 that Tβ4 increased hair growth through activation of hair follicle stem cells in mice [20]. A 2007 follow-up from the same group described hair growth through stem cell migration and differentiation [21]. A third 2004 paper by Philp, Goldstein and Kleinman reviewed the peptide's effects on angiogenesis, wound healing and hair follicle development [24], and a 2010 study of Tβ4 over-expression in mice reported both abnormal tooth development and stimulation of hair growth [25].

Grokipedia's summary says the hair findings come from rodent studies only, that no reliable human trials exist, and that no evidence supports use for alopecia areata [13]. These models used normal hair cycling in healthy animals.

Phase 2 trials reported by sponsors include pressure ulcers, venous stasis ulcers (about 72 participants), epidermolysis bullosa (30, terminated), corneal wounds in diabetes (12, terminated) and dry eye (72) [5][6][7][8][11][12]. Wikipedia describes faster wound repair and good tolerability in the wound trials and improvement in dry eye and neurotrophic keratopathy that lasted after treatment [2]. Grokipedia's summary says the venous ulcer results were not conclusively better than placebo, that a pressure-ulcer Phase 2 involving 143 patients shortened healing by about a month, and that a Phase 3 ophthalmic trial (SEER-3, reported July 2025) missed its primary endpoint for complete corneal healing while secondary outcomes suggested tolerability [13].

Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers were completed [14][15][16]. Cardiac work includes small pilot reports in myocardial infarction, two withdrawn registered trials and a new Phase 2 registered for 2026 [13][17][18]. No trial of hair growth in people was found.

TB-500 is a synthetic version of an active region of Tβ4; a cited 2012 study describes a method for detecting it in equine samples, and Grokipedia reports that a 2024 study suggested its wound-healing activity may come from a metabolite, Ac-LKKTE [2][13]. Descriptions of its length vary between sources [13].

It is sold online as a research product. Grokipedia describes widespread sales through online vendors, with reports of impurities, counterfeits and inconsistent labelling, and says evidence for absorption from oral capsules is poor [13]. That source also reports that the FDA placed TB-500 in its Category 2 for compounding in 2023 and that reclassification was being discussed in 2026; as an AI-written page it should be read with care [13].

On looksmax.org Tβ4 appears mainly as TB-500, usually paired with BPC-157 in what users call a 'wolverine stack'. In one German-language thread a member asks about combining the two, and a reply says they had used both for recovery around surgery and after a gym injury, while another suggests a copper-peptide alternative [26]. Another thread weighs peptides such as TB-500 for muscle growth and recovery with the question 'cope or not' [27].

A thread titled as a guide proposes combining BPC-157 and TB-500 to remodel facial sutures, with the author claiming about 1.5 mm wider cheekbones over a year measured by DEXA; some replies compare it to bonesmashing and ask whether it worked [22]. No published study supports peptide-driven facial bone change in adults, and the post is best read as a community claim.

WADA prohibits Tβ4 and derivatives such as TB-500 because the peptide might aid soft-tissue recovery and permit higher training loads [2][13]. In the 2010s players from the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks (NRL) and Essendon (AFL) were found guilty of doping in cases linked to a program run by sports scientist Stephen Dank [2][28].

The Essendon sequence began in November 2011 when Dank's supplements program started. Essendon self-reported to the AFL and ASADA on 5 February 2013, and the Australian Crime Commission released its report two days later [23]. On 12 June 2014 ASADA issued show-cause notices to 34 players alleging use of Tβ4 [23]. The AFL Tribunal found all 34 not guilty on 31 March 2015, accepting that Tβ4 was banned but not being comfortably satisfied it had been administered [23]. After WADA appealed, the Court of Arbitration for Sport found the 34 players guilty on 12 January 2016 and imposed two-year bans backdated to March 2015; the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed the players' appeal on 11 October 2016 [23]. Dank received a lifetime ban in 2015, and a jury in his 2016 defamation suit found most accusations against him substantially true [23][28].
Tβ4 holds no FDA or EMA approval. Grokipedia reports an FDA orphan drug designation for neurotrophic keratopathy on 31 December 2013 [13].

Trials reported mild effects, such as injection-site reactions and fatigue at rates similar to placebo, and no serious adverse events, but trials lasted weeks to months and long-term data are lacking [13]. Because the peptide promotes blood-vessel growth and has been discussed in cancer metastasis research, tumour promotion is described as a theoretical concern, with no causal link shown in human trials [13]. Pediatric safety has not been established [13]. One looksmax.org poster asking about BPC-157 mentions having heard it could support tumour growth, showing the concern circulates among users [26].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org Tβ4 is discussed almost entirely as TB-500, paired with BPC-157 for injury recovery, with an outlying thread proposing facial remodelling [26][27][22].

claims.claim: TB-500 speeds recovery from injuries and surgery, so users can train more.
claims.believers: A member says he used it with BPC-157 during surgery recovery and after a gym injury; another asker describes pain recurring at the same spot in the same exercises and wants to try it [26].
claims.experts: Phase 2 trials in ulcers and eye wounds reported faster repair and good tolerability, but trials were in specific wound types and TB-500 itself has little human data [2][13].

claims.claim: Thymosin beta-4 regrows or thickens hair.
claims.believers: Users cite the mouse follicle studies as the reason the peptide is discussed for hair [20][21].
claims.experts: Published hair findings are from healthy mice and rats; no human hair trial has been published and no evidence supports use for alopecia areata [20][13].

claims.claim: BPC-157 plus TB-500 can widen cheekbones and densify bone in people under 25.
claims.believers: The author of a guide thread reports 1.5 mm wider cheekbones and 10 percent more jaw density in 12 months on a DEXA scan, citing orthopaedic and wound-care papers [22].
claims.experts: No published study has examined facial suture or skull remodelling in healthy people with these peptides, and the post's measurements have not been independently verified.

claims.claim: The 'wolverine stack' of BPC-157 and TB-500 is the standard recovery pairing.
claims.believers: A thread titled around the stack asks about combining the two, and a replier says he cycled both for recovery [26].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the combination in humans.

claims.believers: A thread asks whether peptides for muscle growth and recovery such as TB-500 are worth it or 'cope' [27].
claims.experts: WADA bans the peptide because it may aid soft-tissue recovery and allow higher training loads [2][13]; no trial has measured muscle gain.

claims.claim: Gray-market peptide vials are what they say they are.
claims.believers: Threads discuss buying peptides as research products and ask about starting them [26].
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports impurities, counterfeits and inconsistent labelling among unregulated sellers [13].

card.summary: A natural actin-binding peptide with wound and eye trials and mouse hair data; sold as TB-500, banned in sport.
card.note: Not approved; no human hair trials; WADA-prohibited.

quick.overview:
Thymosin beta-4 is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide that regulates actin in cells. Phase 2 trials tested it for skin ulcers and eye conditions, with mixed or incomplete results reported.

Hair-growth claims rest on mouse studies. It circulates online as a research peptide, along with the fragment TB-500.
quick.mechanism: It binds monomeric actin to control cell structure and movement, and is reported to promote cell migration and new blood vessels outside cells.
quick.risks: Trials reported mild effects, but long-term data are lacking. Its blood-vessel-promoting activity raises theoretical tumor concerns. It is unapproved, WADA-prohibited, and gray-market products vary in purity.

chain: Peptide reported to promote cell migration, blood-vessel growth and tissue repair
Users aim for faster recovery and fewer training breaks
More consistent training, or (from mouse hair studies) more hair growth
angle.text: People who use Tβ4 or TB-500 describe it as a healing peptide that helps them train through injuries, and some discuss it for hair, based on rodent follicle studies [20][21][22]. No human trial of its effect on appearance has been published.
